# Corporate engineering standards

Three references, read the one that applies:

- `references/coding-standards.md` — typing, documentation, testing and linting
  requirements per language.
- `references/git-workflow.md` — branch naming, commit format, pull request and
  review rules.
- `references/security-policies.md` — credential handling, dependency policy and
  what must never reach a repository.

When a project's own AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md contradicts these, the project wins:
it is closer to the code. Say so explicitly instead of silently picking one.

# OpenCode Enterprise Config Server One corporate OpenCode configuration, served to every employee's harness over the mechanism OpenCode v2 already ships: the `/.well-known/opencode` manifest. - **Nothing local is ever overwritten.** The harness ranks a well-known document as its *lowest* priority source, below `~/.config/opencode` and below any project config. Nothing is written to the employee's disk to deliver settings. - **Agents, commands, skills, MCP servers, permissions and plugins** all travel as data. Only tooling that must exist as a local binary needs the installer. - **Static credentials**: a username and password, or an API key. No identity provider, no OAuth round trip. - **Changes land within 10 minutes**, in running sessions, with no restart and no re-login. --- ## Run it locally in five minutes ```bash git clone && cd opencode-config-server python -m venv .venv && . .venv/bin/activate pip install -r requirements-dev.txt # 1. Create an account. The command prints a hash; paste it into users.json. cp config/users.json.example config/users.json python -m opencode_config_server.passwd ana.ruiz # 2. Start the server. OCS_BASE_URL=http://localhost:8000 python main.py ``` Check it in another terminal: ```bash curl -fsS http://localhost:8000/health # {"status":"healthy","service":"opencode-enterprise-config","users":1,"skills":1,"problems":[]} ``` `status: "degraded"` is not a failure — `problems` tells you exactly what to fix (no accounts yet, an unparseable config, a missing signing secret). Now connect a machine that has OpenCode v2: ```bash opencode auth login http://localhost:8000 # macOS, Linux opencode auth login http://localhost:8000/windows # Windows ``` Windows has no bash, so its address serves a manifest whose login runs in Windows PowerShell 5.1 instead; everything else is identical. OpenCode prints a sign-in address and a code, and opens the browser when it can. The employee signs in there — username and password, a corporate API key, or a Bifrost virtual key — and OpenCode finishes on its own: ``` │ opencode-corp: sign in from your browser to finish the login: │ opencode-corp: http://localhost:8000/login?code=U86XN7R8 │ opencode-corp: code: U86X-N7R8 ◆ Connected to localhost ``` That is the whole employee experience. Their own settings keep winning; the corporate ones fill in everything they have not set. **Machines without a browser** (CI, build agents) skip the browser by providing a credential up front, in this order of precedence: `OPENCODE_CORP_TOKEN` (an API key), then `OPENCODE_CORP_USER` + `OPENCODE_CORP_PASSWORD`, then a `~/.config/opencode-corp/credentials` file (mode `600`). Mind *where* those variables live: the login command is started by the OpenCode **server**, with the server's environment. Exported in your shell they only reach it with `opencode auth login --standalone`, which starts a private server from that shell. `OPENCODE_CORP_NO_BROWSER=1` prints the address without trying to open it.
If the login fails — the four things it is, almost always | What you see | What it is | | --- | --- | | `Failed to load wellknown manifest` | the server is unreachable, or you put `/.well-known/opencode` behind auth — it must be public, it is what explains *how* to authenticate | | `No authentication method found at …` | the manifest has no `auth` block | | `Authentication command returned no credential` | the login script printed nothing on stdout. Its stderr is in the TUI and says why: a world-readable credentials file, a rejected password | | `the login code expired before it was approved` | nobody signed in at the printed address within `OCS_DEVICE_TTL` (5 minutes by default); run the login again | | login works, no corporate settings appear | the token is being rejected by `/config/opencode.json`. Check `OCS_SESSION_ENV` matches the `{env:…}` placeholder in `config/opencode.jsonc` |
## Going to production ```bash cp .env.example .env python -m opencode_config_server.secret >> .env # OCS_SESSION_SECRET $EDITOR .env # OCS_BASE_URL must be https:// docker compose up -d curl -fsS https://cfg.corp.example/health ``` The server refuses to start with `OCS_ENV=production` unless the base URL is `https` and a signing secret is set — session tokens travel in headers and inside skill URLs, so plain HTTP would hand them to anyone on the path. TLS terminates in front of the container; the app itself listens on `127.0.0.1:8000`. Full checklist in [`docs/SECURITY.md`](docs/SECURITY.md#hardening-checklist). ## The admin panel Set `OCS_ADMIN_TOKEN` and open `/admin`: a web panel for everything below, without touching the files by hand. ```bash python -m opencode_config_server.secret --admin >> .env # OCS_ADMIN_TOKEN docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.admin.yml up -d ``` | Section | What it edits | | --- | --- | | Configuration | `opencode.jsonc` through forms — model and defaults, agents, slash commands, MCP servers, permissions and policies, plugins — or as raw text in the Advanced tab, where comments survive | | Users | create accounts, set passwords, generate API keys (shown once) or register an existing one — e.g. the employee's Bifrost virtual key, so one key serves both — disable, sign out everywhere, delete | | Variables | values for `{env:NAME}`, for everyone or per employee — e.g. each person's own provider key, so it is never written in the file ([guide](docs/VARIABLES.md)) | | Skills | create skills, edit their files, see what is published and at which version | | Installer | `bootstrap/install.sh`, checked with `bash -n` before it is saved | It writes the same files you would edit by hand, so both keep working. Every save is checked first (the shapes OpenCode v2 accepts, `{file:~/.ssh…}` refused, literal secrets in MCP headers flagged), written atomically, refused if someone else changed the file meanwhile, and the previous version is kept in `config/.history` with a one-click restore. Without `OCS_ADMIN_TOKEN` the panel is not mounted at all. Details in [`docs/OPERATIONS.md`](docs/OPERATIONS.md#the-admin-panel) and [`docs/SECURITY.md`](docs/SECURITY.md#the-admin-panel). ## Day-to-day: I want X, I do Y | I want to… | Do this | | --- | --- | | add an employee | `python -m opencode_config_server.passwd `, paste the hash into `config/users.json` | | add a CI or headless account | `python -m opencode_config_server.passwd --api-key`, paste the digest, hand the key over once | | revoke one person's tokens | bump their `version` in `users.json` | | suspend someone | `"disabled": true` | | revoke absolutely everyone | rotate `OCS_SESSION_SECRET` | | change a corporate default | edit `config/opencode.jsonc` | | publish engineering standards | drop a `SKILL.md` in `config/skills//` | | install a tool on every machine | add a step to `config/bootstrap/install.sh` and bump its `VERSION` | Everything above takes effect without a restart: `users.json` on the next request, the configuration and skills on each client's next refresh. Each row also has a button in the [admin panel](#the-admin-panel). ## What can be delivered, and who wins | Need | Where it goes | If the employee also sets it | | --- | --- | --- | | Agents (prompt, model, mode) | `agents.` | they win, field by field | | Slash commands | `commands..template` | theirs wins by name | | Skills (standards, docs, runbooks) | `config/skills/`, served over HTTP | theirs wins by name | | MCP servers | `mcp.servers.` | theirs wins by name | | Permission rules | `permissions[]`, accumulated | their rule is evaluated last | | Providers and models | `providers.` | they win, field by field | | Plugins | `plugins[]`, npm specs, auto-installed | they can remove yours with `"-"` | | `model`, `share`, `experimental`, … | top-level keys | **all or nothing** — if they set the key, your value is ignored entirely | That last row is the one to design around: scalar keys cannot be partially imposed. And because local always wins, an employee *can* opt out of anything, including your plugin. If a setting has to be mandatory, enforce it outside OpenCode — MDM, a managed image, CI. The two properties cannot both hold. ## How it works ``` employee this server │ opencode auth login https://cfg.corp ├─── GET /.well-known/opencode ──────────▶ public manifest, no secrets │◀── {auth:{command,env}, remote_config} ─ │ │ runs auth.command: bash, no shell profile, stdin closed ├─── POST /auth/device ──────────────────▶ login code, nobody signed in yet │◀── {device_code, user_code, …} ──────── │ prints /login?code=… — the employee signs in in a browser, │ which posts the code + credentials to /login/approve ├─── POST /auth/device/token (polls) ────▶ answered once the code is approved │◀── {"token":"v1.…"} ─────────────────── signed, stateless, 90 days │ (CI: POST /auth/token with the credential instead of the browser) │ runs the bootstrap installer (hindsight, …) │ prints the token on stdout → stored by the harness as a credential │ │ on startup, every 10 minutes, and on every config reload: ├─── GET /config/opencode.json ──────────▶ Bearer │◀── the corporate configuration ───────── ├─── GET /skills//index.json ─────▶ token in the path, see below │◀── skills, cached and versioned ──────── ``` | Method | Path | Auth | Purpose | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `GET` | `/.well-known/opencode` | none | discovery manifest | | `POST` | `/auth/token` | Basic or `X-Api-Key` | static credentials → session token | | `POST` | `/auth/device` | none | start a browser login: device code + user code | | `POST` | `/auth/device/token` | device code | polled; the session token once the code is approved | | `GET` | `/login` | none | the browser sign-in page | | `POST` | `/login/approve` | credentials in body | approve a user code with a password, API key or Bifrost key | | `GET` | `/config/opencode.json` | `Bearer` | the corporate configuration | | `GET` | `/skills/{token}/index.json` | token in path | remote skill index | | `GET` | `/skills/{token}/{name}/{file}` | token in path | remote skill file | | `GET` | `/bootstrap/install.sh` | `Bearer` | one-off installer | | `GET` | `/health` | none | self-check, no secrets | ### Three constraints the harness imposes Worth knowing before you debug anything, and all three are verified by tests: 1. **The manifest must be public.** `inspect()` fetches it with no credentials ([`wellknown.ts:60`][wellknown]) — it is the thing that tells a client how to authenticate. 2. **The login command's stdout *is* the credential**, trimmed ([`integration.ts:620-650`][integration]). It runs through execve with no shell and with stdin closed, so it cannot prompt, and `bash -l` is out: a chatty shell profile would end up inside the token. The script routes everything to stderr and keeps the token on a separate descriptor. 3. **Skill downloads carry no headers at all** ([`skill/discovery.ts`][skills]), so the token rides in the URL path. A query string would be dropped. It will therefore appear in proxy access logs — redact `/skills/`, or set `OCS_SKILLS_ENABLED=false` and ship standards through the installer instead. [`docs/PROTOCOL.md`](docs/PROTOCOL.md) has the rest, read off the v2 sources with file and line references: merge regimes per key, why `version` is mandatory in the skill index, what `{file:…}` does and does not do, and how v1 differs. ## What IT edits ``` config/ opencode.jsonc the corporate configuration (JSON with comments) users.json accounts: password hashes, API key digests, revocation skills//SKILL.md skills delivered over HTTP, never installed on disk bootstrap/install.sh third-party tooling that must exist as a local binary ``` Placeholders: `{server_url}` and `{session_token}` are resolved here; `{env:NAME}` is filled in here when the Variables page defines `NAME` for that employee, and otherwise left, like `{file:path}`, for OpenCode to resolve on the employee's machine. All of it in [`docs/VARIABLES.md`](docs/VARIABLES.md). > Write access to `config/` is equivalent to code execution on every employee's > machine — `plugins[]` runs in their harness, `install.sh` runs on their shell. > Review changes to it like you review code. ## Tests ```bash pytest # 299 tests pytest tests/test_login_e2e.py # the real login script against a real server pytest tests/test_harness_schema.py # the served document against OpenCode's own schema ``` Two suites check more than our own assumptions: - `test_login_e2e.py` boots the app on a loopback port and runs the exact `auth.command` from the manifest with a temporary `HOME`: only the token on stdout, progress on stderr, the right exit code per failure, and a broken installer that does not cost the employee their session. - `test_harness_schema.py` feeds the served document to OpenCode's own `ConfigNormalize.normalize` and `Schema.decodeUnknownOption(Info)` and demands zero diagnostics — proof the harness is not silently dropping half of it. Needs `bun` and an OpenCode checkout (`OPENCODE_SOURCE=…`); skips itself otherwise. ## Documentation | | | | --- | --- | | [`docs/PROTOCOL.md`](docs/PROTOCOL.md) | the harness contract, verified against the v2 sources, with `file:line` references | | [`docs/VARIABLES.md`](docs/VARIABLES.md) | the placeholders you can use, per-employee values, provider keys and Bifrost as the LLM gateway | | [`docs/OPERATIONS.md`](docs/OPERATIONS.md) | the admin panel, accounts, revocation, publishing skills, rotating secrets, troubleshooting | | [`docs/SECURITY.md`](docs/SECURITY.md) | trust model, what a leaked token buys, hardening checklist | | [`docs/MIGRATION.md`](docs/MIGRATION.md) | what changed from 1.x and why that design could not work | | [`DEVELOPMENT.md`](DEVELOPMENT.md) | layout, conventions, where to add a test | `legacy/` holds the 1.x implementation for reference. `examples/opencode.full.jsonc` is a large real-world configuration to crib from — review it before serving it, it carries absolute paths from one workstation. [wellknown]: https://github.com/sst/opencode/blob/dev/packages/core/src/wellknown.ts [integration]: https://github.com/sst/opencode/blob/dev/packages/core/src/integration.ts [skills]: https://github.com/sst/opencode/blob/dev/packages/core/src/skill/discovery.ts

# Development

```bash
python -m venv .venv && . .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements-dev.txt

cp config/users.json.example config/users.json
python -m opencode_config_server.passwd dev        # paste the hash in
OCS_BASE_URL=http://localhost:8000 python main.py
```

`OCS_ENV` defaults to `development`, which generates a throwaway signing secret
on each start. Tokens stop working on restart; `/health` says so.

## Layout

```
opencode_config_server/
  app.py            routes, auth dependencies, error mapping
  auth.py           password hashing, API keys, signed session tokens, rate limit
  manifest.py       the /.well-known/opencode document
  login_script.sh   what the harness executes on login (inlined into the manifest)
  configdoc.py      reads config/opencode.jsonc, injects server-side placeholders
  skills.py         index.json and file serving for remote skills
  jsonc.py          JSON with comments and trailing commas
  settings.py       environment-driven settings, with production guards
  passwd.py         `python -m opencode_config_server.passwd`
  secret.py         `python -m opencode_config_server.secret`
config/             what IT edits; mounted read-only in production
legacy/             the 1.x implementation, kept for reference only
```

## Tests

```bash
pytest                              # everything, ~4s
pytest tests/test_login_e2e.py -v   # the real login script against a real server
pytest -k manifest                  # the harness contract
```

`tests/test_login_e2e.py` boots uvicorn on a loopback port and runs the exact
argv from the manifest with a temporary `HOME`. It needs `bash` and `curl`, and
skips itself when either is missing.

### Where to add a test

| Change | Test to extend |
| --- | --- |
| the manifest shape | `test_manifest.py` — `assert_decodes_as_v2_manifest` mirrors the harness schema |
| the login script | `test_login_e2e.py`, and the string assertions in `test_manifest.py` |
| credentials or tokens | `test_auth_token.py`, `test_session_tokens.py` |
| the corporate document | `test_config_endpoint.py` |
| skills | `test_skills.py`, plus `TestSkillPathSafety` in `test_health_and_settings.py` |
| anything read at runtime from a new file | `test_packaging.py` — it proves the file reaches the image |

## Conventions

- No `from __future__ import annotations` in `app.py`: FastAPI resolves string
  annotations against module globals, and the dependencies there are closures
  over `create_app` locals. With deferred annotations FastAPI stops seeing the
  `Depends(...)` markers and treats them as query parameters — every
  authenticated endpoint starts answering `422`.
- Dependencies stay minimal: `fastapi` and `uvicorn`. Tokens are stdlib HMAC.
- Anything asserted about the harness belongs in `docs/PROTOCOL.md` with a
  `file:line` reference to the opencode sources, not in a comment.

# Migrating from the 1.x design

The 1.x server implemented a protocol the harness does not have. It could not
work against OpenCode v2 in any configuration, and the test suite passed anyway
because every test asserted the invented protocol instead of the real one. The
original files are kept under `legacy/` for reference.

## What was wrong

| 1.x | Reality |
| --- | --- |
| `auth: {type: "command", command: "<string>"}` | `auth: {command: string[], env: string}` — a string fails the schema, so `opencode auth login` dies on "Failed to load wellknown manifest" |
| `/.well-known/opencode` behind `Authorization: Bearer` | the harness fetches it with no credentials; the endpoint that explains how to authenticate cannot require authentication |
| served `config.json` | v2 reads `opencode.json` / `opencode.jsonc` |
| token interpolated into a shell string and passed as `argv` | command injection through the `Authorization` header, and the token visible in `ps` |
| `len(token) >= 10` as the auth check | any ten characters read the whole configuration |
| `bundle.tar.gz` + SHA-256 state + `merge.py` writing into `~/.config/opencode` | unnecessary: the harness already ranks remote config *below* local files and re-fetches every 10 minutes |
| `merge.py` rewriting `~/.opencode.env` | dropped every line that was not `export …`, and wrote `export KEY=${KEY:-}` — self-referential, so the "injected" secrets were always empty |
| `merge.py` never copied into the Docker image | `/cdn/merge.py` answered 404 in every container, breaking login entirely |

## Conceptual change

1.x pushed files onto the employee's disk and tried to merge them with a
"user wins" strategy written by hand. 2.x pushes **data** and lets the harness do
the merging, which it already does correctly:

| 1.x delivery | 2.x delivery |
| --- | --- |
| `config.json` written into `~/.config/opencode` | `GET /config/opencode.json`, loaded as the lowest-priority document |
| `rules/*.md` copied if absent | a skill served over HTTP, cached and versioned by the harness |
| `~/.omo/config.yaml` deep-merged by a script | out of scope: third-party tool config belongs to the bootstrap installer |
| `~/.opencode.env` rewritten | out of scope: the server never had those secrets anyway |
| `bootstrap.sh` doing merge + sync + shell-rc injection | `bootstrap/install.sh`, only for tooling that must exist as a local binary |

Nothing in 2.x writes to `~/.config/opencode`, so there is nothing to merge and
nothing to overwrite.

## What carried over

- `config_root/rules/*.md` became `config/skills/corp-standards/references/*.md`,
  delivered as a skill.
- `config_root/opencode.jsonc`, the large real-world configuration, is kept
  verbatim at `examples/opencode.full.jsonc`. **Review it before serving it**: it
  contains absolute paths from one workstation (for example a local plugin path
  under `/home/…`) that will not exist on an employee's machine.
- The Dockerfile and compose file were rewritten but keep the same shape.

## If you deployed 1.x

Employees who ran the old bootstrap have files on disk that 2.x will not remove:

```
~/.config/opencode/.enterprise_hash     stale, safe to delete
~/.config/opencode/config.json          merged by the old script; v2 ignores the
                                        filename, but check it for corporate
                                        values you no longer want pinned locally
~/.opencode.env                         contains `export KEY=${KEY:-}` lines
~/.bashrc, ~/.zshrc                     one sourcing line for ~/.opencode.env
~/.omo/config.yaml                      merged by the old script
```

None of it breaks 2.x. The one that matters is `~/.config/opencode/config.json`:
anything the old merge wrote there is now *higher* priority than the corporate
document, so an employee can be pinned to an old corporate value without knowing
it. Tell them to delete the keys they did not choose themselves.

# Operations

## Deploying

```bash
cp .env.example .env
python -m opencode_config_server.secret >> .env     # OCS_SESSION_SECRET
$EDITOR .env                                        # OCS_BASE_URL must be https
cp config/users.json.example config/users.json
docker compose up -d
curl -fsS https://cfg.corp/health | jq
```

`/health` is the deployment self-check. `status: "degraded"` lists exactly what
is wrong — a missing user database, an unparseable corporate document, an
ephemeral signing secret — without revealing any of it to an attacker.

TLS terminates in front of the container; the app speaks plain HTTP on
`127.0.0.1:8000`. The server refuses to start with `OCS_ENV=production` unless
`OCS_BASE_URL` is `https://` and `OCS_SESSION_SECRET` is set.

## The admin panel

`/admin` is a web panel over the same files this document describes. It is
mounted only when `OCS_ADMIN_TOKEN` is set:

```bash
python -m opencode_config_server.secret --admin >> .env   # OCS_ADMIN_TOKEN
sudo chown -R 1000:1000 config                            # the container's user
docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.admin.yml up -d
```

The override remounts `config/` read-write; the default compose file keeps it
read-only, which is still the right choice when the panel is off. Without write
access the panel opens in read-only mode and says which file it cannot change.

Sign in with the token. The browser gets a session cookie that lasts
`OCS_ADMIN_SESSION_HOURS` (8 by default, 1–24); scripts send the token as
`Authorization: Bearer …` to the same JSON API under `/admin/api/`.

| Section | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| Configuration | Forms for model and defaults, agents, commands, MCP servers, permissions and policies, plugins. Saving from a form rewrites `opencode.jsonc` as plain JSON, so its comments go (the panel asks first); the **Advanced** tab edits the file as text and keeps them. **Check & preview** shows the document exactly as employees receive it. |
| Users | A generated API key is shown once; only its digest is stored and the panel identifies keys by a short fingerprint. **Register an existing key** instead to reuse one issued elsewhere — typically the employee's Bifrost virtual key, so the same key opens Bifrost and this server (see [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md#bifrost-virtual-keys)). A key can belong to one account only. **Sign out everywhere** bumps `version`. Unknown fields in `users.json` are preserved. A `users.json` that does not parse is never overwritten: fix it by hand first. |
| Skills | Only small text files with a published extension can be created or edited; other files in a skill folder are listed but never shown. Each save changes the skill's version, so employees re-download it. |
| Installer | Refused if `bash -n` reports a syntax error. |

**Every save** is validated, written atomically (temp file + rename), refused
with "changed since it was loaded" when the file changed after the editor opened
it, and the replaced version goes to `config/.history/` — the last 30 per file,
restorable from each section's **History** button. Old versions of `users.json`
can be restored but are never displayed, since they hold password hashes.

Every change is logged as `admin <action> from <ip>`. There is one shared admin
token, so the log tells you what changed and from where, not who: put the panel
behind your SSO proxy if you need per-person attribution.

## Accounts

`config/users.json`:

```json
{
  "users": [
    { "name": "ana.ruiz", "password": "pbkdf2_sha256$600000$…$…", "version": 1 },
    { "name": "ci-runner", "api_keys": ["sha256:…"], "version": 1 }
  ]
}
```

| Task | How |
| --- | --- |
| Add a password account | `python -m opencode_config_server.passwd ana.ruiz`, paste the hash |
| Add an API key | `python -m opencode_config_server.passwd --api-key`, paste the digest, hand the key over once |
| Revoke one employee's tokens | bump their `version` |
| Suspend an account | `"disabled": true` |
| Remove an account | delete the entry |

All of these take effect on the **next request** — no restart. A revoked or
deleted account loses access to the configuration and to the skill feed
immediately; the employee's next login gets a fresh token.

Plaintext in the `password` field is rejected, loudly: the server answers `503`
and logs the offending user rather than authenticating anyone.

No `users.json` at all is a valid state: a fresh server (the first user added
in the admin panel creates it), or a company that signs in only with Bifrost
virtual keys, which work without it. Passwords and local API keys then get a
`503` rather than a `401`, so a file that went missing by accident never reads
as "wrong password" to every employee.

A broken `users.json` keeps the last good snapshot in memory and logs an error,
so a typo during an edit does not lock the company out. If there is no usable
snapshot at all, `/auth/token` answers `503` — never `401`, which would send
employees chasing their own passwords.

## The corporate configuration

`config/opencode.jsonc` is JSON with comments and trailing commas, like the
harness's own config files. Two placeholders are resolved server side:

| Placeholder | Becomes |
| --- | --- |
| `{server_url}` | `OCS_BASE_URL` |
| `{session_token}` | `{env:OPENCODE_CORP_SESSION}`, filled in on the employee's machine |

`{env:NAME}` and `{file:path}` are passed through untouched for the harness to
resolve locally.

Remember the priority rules from [PROTOCOL.md](PROTOCOL.md#4-priority-local-always-wins):
scalar keys like `model` are all-or-nothing, while `agents`, `commands`,
`permissions`, `mcp.servers`, `skills` and `plugins` merge. Set a corporate
`model` and any employee who has their own `model` ignores yours entirely —
usually what you want, occasionally a surprise.

Changes reach running sessions within 10 minutes. Nothing to restart, nothing to
re-login.

## Publishing a skill

```
config/skills/<name>/SKILL.md          required (or <name>.md)
config/skills/<name>/references/*.md   optional, any depth
```

`SKILL.md` needs YAML frontmatter with `name` and `description`; the description
is what makes the harness load it, so describe *when* to use it, not just what
it is.

Published suffixes: `.md .txt .json .yaml .yml .toml .csv .py .sh .js .ts`, up
to 2 MB each. Anything else in the directory — a `.key`, a `.png`, a dotfile —
stays private.

Versions come from a content hash, so an edit invalidates the employee's cache
automatically. A skill directory without an entry file is skipped rather than
served broken.

Verify what clients will see:

```bash
TOKEN=$(curl -fsS -X POST -H "X-Api-Key: $KEY" https://cfg.corp/auth/token | jq -r .token)
curl -fsS "https://cfg.corp/skills/$TOKEN/index.json" | jq
```

## The bootstrap installer

`config/bootstrap/install.sh` runs once per employee, on login, for things that
must exist as local binaries. The shipped version installs `hindsight`.

Windows machines run `config/bootstrap/install.ps1` instead (Windows PowerShell
5.1, `$args[0]` is the server URL), served at `/bootstrap/install.ps1`. The
admin panel edits both, one tab each; `install.ps1` is checked with PowerShell's
own parser when `pwsh` is installed on the server. A machine only ever runs the
one for its platform, so keep the two equivalent.

Three rules, enforced by tests:

- **Idempotent.** It runs again on every fresh login; the version stamp in
  `~/.local/state/opencode-corp/bootstrap.version` short-circuits it.
- **Never fatal.** It runs without `set -e`, and the login survives a failed
  step with a warning. An employee must never lose their session to a broken
  installer.
- **Bump `VERSION`** when you change the steps, or clients that already ran it
  will skip the new ones.

Its stdout is already redirected to stderr by the caller, so it can print
freely; the session token travels on a separate descriptor and cannot be
corrupted by it.

Set `OCS_BOOTSTRAP_ENABLED=false` to stop serving it entirely.

## Rotating the signing secret

Rotating `OCS_SESSION_SECRET` invalidates **every** issued token at once. Each
employee's next config refresh fails with a logged warning and they must run
`opencode auth login` again. Do it on compromise, not on a schedule.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause |
| --- | --- |
| `opencode auth login` fails with "Failed to load wellknown manifest" | `/.well-known/opencode` unreachable, or behind auth — it must be public |
| "No authentication method found at …" | the manifest has no `auth` block |
| Login fails with "Authentication command returned no credential" | the login script printed nothing on stdout; check its stderr in the TUI |
| "the login code expired before it was approved" | nobody signed in at the printed address in time; raise `OCS_DEVICE_TTL` (max 540 s) if employees need longer |
| The browser does not open | the OpenCode server has no `DISPLAY`/`WAYLAND_DISPLAY` (a headless service); the address is printed, open it by hand |
| "Bifrost virtual keys are not accepted by this server" | `OCS_BIFROST_URL` is not set |
| "cannot validate the virtual key right now (Bifrost unavailable)" (`503`) | `OCS_BIFROST_URL` unreachable, or Bifrost answered something other than 200/401/403 |
| Windows login fails with exit code 9 | `/login.ps1` changed between fetching the manifest and the script (a deploy in between); run the login again |
| Windows login: "powershell" not found | the machine has no Windows PowerShell 5.1 on `PATH`; it ships with Windows 10/11 |
| The panel says a file is read-only | `config/` is mounted `:ro`, or not owned by uid 1000 inside the container; use `docker-compose.admin.yml` and `chown` |
| "changed since it was loaded" when saving in the panel | another admin, or a hand edit, saved the file after you opened it; reload and redo the change |
| `/admin` answers 404 | `OCS_ADMIN_TOKEN` is not set |
| A CI login waits for a browser instead of using its credential | the credential variables are not in the OpenCode server's environment; use `opencode auth login --standalone` |
| Login succeeds but no corporate settings appear | the token is rejected by `/config/opencode.json`; check `OCS_SESSION_ENV` matches the `{env:…}` in the document |
| Skills never update | the index is served without `version`, or the employee's cache under `~/.cache/opencode/skills` predates it |
| Everything works for one employee and not another | the other employee has the same keys set locally — local wins, by design |

Server logs record the subject of every issued token, every rejection and every
served document. They never record a token, a password or a hash.

## Operational limits

- The rate limiter is per process and in memory. Behind more than one replica,
  or for a real lockout policy, do it at the edge.
- The admin panel serialises writes per process. Two replicas editing the same
  file are still caught by the ETag check, but run the panel on one replica.
- Pending browser logins are in memory too. A restart, or a second replica
  answering the poll, costs the employee a retry of `opencode auth login`; run
  one replica, or pin `/auth/device*` and `/login*` to one.
- `OCS_TRUST_PROXY=true` makes the limiter believe `X-Forwarded-For`. Enable it
  only when the proxy in front sets that header itself, otherwise any client can
  forge its own bucket.

# The harness contract

Everything here was read off the OpenCode v2 sources (v2.0.14) rather than
inferred from documentation. Paths are relative to the opencode repository.

## 1. Discovery

`packages/core/src/wellknown.ts:12-32`

```ts
Auth         = Schema.Struct({ command: Schema.Array(Schema.String), env: Schema.String })
RemoteConfig = Schema.Struct({ url: Schema.String, headers: Schema.optional(Record(String,String)) })
Manifest     = Schema.Struct({ auth: optional(Auth), config: optional(NullOr(Config)), remote_config: optional(RemoteConfig) })
```

`inspect()` (`wellknown.ts:60-67`) fetches `<origin>/.well-known/opencode` **with
no credentials**. The endpoint must therefore be public: it is what tells the
client how to authenticate in the first place.

`command` is an argv array, not a command line, and `env` is the *name* of the
variable the token will be exposed as. `add()` (`wellknown.ts:147-158`) refuses
an origin whose manifest has no `auth`, so `opencode auth login` fails outright
on a manifest that misses it.

Our implementation: `opencode_config_server/manifest.py`.

## 2. The login command

`packages/core/src/integration.ts:595-650`

```ts
processes.spawn(ChildProcess.make(method.command[0], method.command.slice(1), {
  extendEnv: true,
  stdin: "ignore",
}))
```

- **execve, no shell.** `["bash", "-c", script, argv0, …args]` is how shell
  logic gets in. `-l` is avoided on purpose: a login shell sources the
  employee's profile, and anything it prints lands in the credential.
- **stdout, trimmed, becomes the credential.** Empty stdout is an error
  ("Authentication command returned no credential").
- **stderr is streamed to the user** as the attempt's message, and is what they
  see when it fails.
- **Non-zero exit fails the login**, with the collected stderr as the message.
- **stdin is `/dev/null`**: the command cannot prompt.
- **The environment is the OpenCode server's**, not the employee's shell
  (`extendEnv: true` on the server process). With the background service,
  variables exported before `opencode auth login` never reach the command;
  `--standalone` starts a private server from the calling shell
  (`packages/cli/src/services/standalone.ts`, also `extendEnv: true`), so there
  they do.
- **Both the CLI and the TUI show stderr live**, one completed line at a time
  (`packages/cli/src/commands/handlers/auth/login.ts`,
  `packages/tui/src/component/dialog-integration.tsx`). That is what makes a
  browser login possible: the command prints an address and a code, then waits.
- **The attempt is abandoned after 10 minutes**, so a login code has to expire
  well before that (`OCS_DEVICE_TTL`, at most 540 s).

Our command therefore signs in through the browser, shaped after RFC 8628:

```
script                         server                          browser
POST /auth/device        ->    device_code + user_code
prints /login?code=…                                     ->    GET /login?code=…
                                                         <-    POST /login/approve
POST /auth/device/token  ->    400 authorization_pending        (password, API key
  … every `interval` s   ->    200 {"token": …}, exactly once    or Bifrost key)
```

The device code is the script's secret and never leaves it; the user code is
what the employee compares in the browser. Polling errors follow RFC 8628 §3.5
(`authorization_pending`, `slow_down`, `expired_token`, `access_denied`). A
credential in the environment or in `~/.config/opencode-corp/credentials`
skips the browser and goes straight to `POST /auth/token` — that is the CI path.

The command runs **only on an explicit login**, never on a refresh. Anything
that must stay current cannot live here.

Our implementation: `opencode_config_server/login_script.sh`, exercised
end-to-end in `tests/test_login_e2e.py`.

### Windows

`bash -c` does not exist on a stock Windows machine, and OpenCode does not tell
the server which OS is asking: the manifest request carries no platform hint.
But `inspect()` builds the manifest URL as `<origin>/.well-known/opencode`
(`wellknown.ts:65-66`), and the origin may carry a path. So Windows machines
run `opencode auth login <server>/windows`, and that manifest's command is
`powershell -NoProfile -NonInteractive -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -Command <launcher>`.

The PowerShell script cannot be inlined like the bash one: Windows command
lines stop at 32,767 characters. The launcher (under 1 KB, single quotes only,
so Windows argument quoting has nothing to mangle) downloads `/login.ps1` and
runs it only if its SHA-256 matches the one written in the manifest; otherwise
it exits 9 without running anything. The manifest stays the one thing to audit.

`login_script.ps1` targets Windows PowerShell 5.1, which every Windows 10/11
machine has, and implements the same contract: browser login, credentials from
the environment or the credentials file, `bootstrap/install.ps1`, the
employee's own variables winning, machine variables through a detached
process. Both manifests point at the same `remote_config`: one configuration
for every platform.

Verified by running it under PowerShell 7 (a container, against a live server):
password and browser logins, the installer's output kept off stdout, own values
kept, machine variables applied. Not yet run on Windows PowerShell 5.1 itself.

## 3. Loading the remote configuration

`packages/core/src/config.ts:145-170`

```ts
const credential = (yield* credentials.list(entry.integrationID)).at(-1)
if (!credential || credential.value.type !== "key") return []
const variables = { [auth.env]: credential.value.key }
const configs = yield* wellknown.resolve(entry, variables)
```

`resolve()` (`wellknown.ts:77-96`) substitutes `{env:NAME}` in the
`remote_config` URL and headers, then fetches it. The fetched document is then
run through `ConfigVariable.substitute` again with the same variables, so
`{env:<auth.env>}` also works *inside* the configuration — that is how the skill
URL gets the employee's token.

Only credentials of type `key` are accepted. There is no refresh path for a
command-issued credential: when the token expires the corporate config silently
stops loading (a logged warning, nothing user-facing). Hence long-lived tokens
plus server-side revocation.

## 4. Priority: local always wins

`packages/core/src/config.ts:229-236`, documented at `config.ts:29`
("*from lowest to highest priority*"):

```
[ wellknown, global(~/.config/opencode), explicit(--config), direct, project, content ]
```

Two different merge regimes apply on top of that ordering:

| Key | Mechanism | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `agents.<id>` | per-field, per document, in order (`config/plugin/agent.ts:95-125`) | corporate defaults, local overrides survive field by field; `update()` creates ids that do not exist |
| `commands.<name>` | `add()` per name (`config/plugin/command.ts:74`) | inline `template`, no files needed |
| `skills[]` | accumulated; http(s) entries become URL sources (`config/plugin/skill.ts:92-95`) | remote skills; same-named skill: last source loaded wins (see §5) |
| `instructions[]` | accumulated and deduplicated (`config/plugin/instruction.ts:144-147`) | an employee can add, not remove |
| `mcp.servers.<name>` | by name, later document wins (`config/plugin/mcp.ts:47-55`) | overridable |
| `plugins[]` | concatenated across documents (`plugin/skill.ts:72-78`) | `"-<pkg>"` removes one (`config/plugin/source.ts:117-119`) |
| `permissions[]` | accumulated with `push`, evaluated `findLast` | corporate rules are a floor, not a lock |
| `model`, `share`, `experimental`, `tool_output`, … | `Config.latest` → `findLast` | **all or nothing**: if the employee sets the key, the corporate value is ignored entirely |

That last row is the one to design around: scalar keys cannot be
*partially* imposed.

## 5. Remote skills

Skill sources from every document are added together
(`config/plugin/skill.ts:80-104`): first the skill folders of each config
directory (`~/.config/opencode/skill(s)`, `.opencode/skill(s)` in the project),
then each document's `skills` list in document order, corporate first. A
skill's identity is its folder name (`skill-file.ts:45-48`), and when two
sources provide the same one **the one loaded last wins** (`skills.set(id, …)`):
a corporate URL source therefore replaces an employee's same-named skill from
their own folders. To keep the employee's, the login command reports the
corporate skill names they also have in `~/.config/opencode/skill(s)` and the
server leaves those out of that employee's index. Project-level folders cannot
be seen at login.

`instructions` work the same way minus the identity: every document's entries
are added together and deduplicated (`config/plugin/instruction.ts:144-167`);
relative entries are searched upwards from each session's directory, URLs are
fetched when the configuration loads (5 s timeout, last good copy kept).


`packages/core/src/skill/discovery.ts:92-200`

```
GET <base>/index.json     -> { skills: [ { name, version?, files: [...] } ] }
GET <base>/<name>/<file>  -> file contents
```

- Cached under `<global.cache>/skills/<hash(base)>/<name>/`.
- **No headers are sent.** The token must ride in the path; a query string is
  dropped by `new URL("index.json", base)`.
- Files whose origin differs from the index origin are refused
  (`discovery.ts:131`), as are unsafe names and paths (`discovery.ts:16-46`).
- A skill without `SKILL.md` or `<name>.md` is dropped.
- **`version` is effectively mandatory.** Without it the branch at
  `discovery.ts:152` only downloads files that are missing, so an employee keeps
  the first copy they ever fetched. We derive it from a content hash
  (`opencode_config_server/skills.py`).

## 6. Refresh cadence

`packages/core/src/config.ts:308-325` re-inspects every manifest every 10
minutes and reloads the configuration. A reload is also triggered by
`credential.switched` and by `wellknown.updated`. No hashes, no state files, no
tarballs: the client simply re-fetches.

## 7. What `{file:…}` does and does not do

`packages/core/src/config/variable.ts:56-58` resolves `{file:…}` against the
local filesystem only — there is no remote fetch. A corporate document cannot
ship file *contents* this way; it can only point at paths that already exist on
the employee's machine. This is also why `configdoc.py` refuses to serve a
document referencing `~/.ssh`, `~/.aws` and friends: the harness would happily
read them and a later `mcp` header could carry them back out.

## 8. OpenCode v1

v1 implements the same discovery with a different auth entry
(`packages/opencode/src/config/config.ts:355-395`): an auth record of type
`wellknown` holding `{key, token}`, and `mergeConfigConcatArrays` instead of the
per-domain merge above. The same manifest works for both: v1 ignores `auth` and
reads `config`/`remote_config`.

## 9. Not usable for this

`enterprise.url` in the config schema (`packages/schema/src/config.ts:44`) is
session-sharing configuration, unrelated to configuration distribution.

# Security model

## What this protects

The corporate configuration document, the skill feed and the bootstrap
installer, all behind static credentials. Everything an authenticated employee
can read, every authenticated employee can read: there is one configuration for
the whole company.

## What is public

Also `/windows/.well-known/opencode` and `/login.ps1`: the Windows manifest and
the PowerShell login script it downloads. The manifest pins the script's
SHA-256, so a script that does not match is never run.

`/.well-known/opencode`, `/health`, the sign-in page `/login`, and the start of
a browser login, `POST /auth/device`.

The manifest has to be public — the harness fetches it with no credentials
(`wellknown.ts:60`), because it is what explains how to authenticate. It
contains the login script and the config URL, and no secret. Treat the script as
published: it is, to anyone who can reach the server.

`/health` reports counts and problem descriptions, never names, hashes or
tokens.

`POST /auth/device` hands out a pair of codes that are worth nothing until
someone approves the user code with valid credentials. The number of pending
logins is capped (1000) and each expires after `OCS_DEVICE_TTL`.

### The browser login

- The **device code** (256 bits) only ever travels between the login command and
  the server; it is what redeems the token, exactly once. The **user code**
  (8 characters from a 27-letter alphabet, ~38 bits) is only good for approving,
  and approving is rate limited like `/auth/token`: a wrong code counts as a
  failed attempt.
- `/login` is a single self-contained page: no external resources, a per-request
  CSP nonce (`default-src 'none'`, `connect-src 'self'`, `frame-ancestors
  'none'`), `X-Frame-Options: DENY`, `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`, and the
  `code` parameter is escaped. Credentials go in a JSON body to
  `/login/approve`, never in a URL.
- The page tells the employee to continue only if they just ran
  `opencode auth login` and the codes match. That is the defence against the
  classic device-flow phish — an attacker starting a login and sending someone
  else the link — and it is a human check, as in every RFC 8628 deployment.

## Credentials

| Artefact | At rest | In transit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Password | PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256, 600 000 iterations, 16-byte salt | HTTP Basic over TLS |
| API key | SHA-256 digest | `X-Api-Key` over TLS |
| Session token | not stored — stateless HMAC-SHA256 | `Authorization: Bearer`, and a URL path segment for skills |
| Bifrost virtual key | not stored here — checked against Bifrost on each sign-in | JSON body to `/login/approve`, or `X-Api-Key`; forwarded to Bifrost as `x-bf-vk` |

Password and API key comparisons use `hmac.compare_digest`. An unknown username
is verified against a dummy hash so it costs the same as a wrong password, and
both return the identical message — there is no account-existence oracle.

### The session token in a URL path

Skill downloads carry no headers, so the token appears in the path. The
consequences are real and bounded:

- It will appear in reverse-proxy access logs. Strip or redact the path for
  `/skills/`, or accept that your logs hold valid credentials.
- It cannot be in a query string instead: the harness drops those when resolving
  the index URL.
- A leaked token reads the configuration and the skills. It cannot write
  anything, cannot escalate, and dies when you bump that user's `version`.

If this is unacceptable, set `OCS_SKILLS_ENABLED=false` and distribute standards
through the bootstrap installer instead.

### Revocation

The harness has no refresh mechanism for a command-issued credential
(`config.ts:148` accepts only `type: "key"`), so tokens are long-lived — 90 days
by default. Revocation is therefore server side and checked on **every** request:

1. signature and expiry (`SessionTokens.verify`)
2. the account still exists
3. the account is not disabled
4. the token's `ver` matches the user's current `version`

Bump `version` to kill one user's tokens; rotate `OCS_SESSION_SECRET` to kill
everyone's.

### Variables

`config/variables.json` (0600) holds the values the server fills into
`{env:NAME}` — typically provider API keys — in clear, like `users.json` holds
password hashes. Each value is sent only to the employee it belongs to, or to
everyone for shared ones. Secret values are write-only in the panel, history
versions of the file are restorable but not viewable, and the log names the
variable, never the value. Values cannot contain `{env:…}` or `{file:…}`.
An employee's own environment always wins: the login reports which of these
names they define themselves (names only), and the server leaves those to their
machine; "machine" variables never overwrite or remove a value the employee set.
Details in [VARIABLES.md](VARIABLES.md#security).

### Bifrost virtual keys

With `OCS_BIFROST_URL` set, a key starting with `sk-bf-` is checked with
Bifrost's self-service `GET /api/governance/virtual-keys/quota` (no admin
credential involved; the key is the credential). It is accepted only on `200`
**and** `"is_active": true` — Bifrost also answers `200` for a key that has been
switched off. `401` (unknown) and `403` (expired) are rejections; anything else,
or Bifrost being unreachable, is a `503`, not a bad credential.

The session belongs to `vk:<virtual key name>`. Those names cannot be created in
`users.json`, so a Bifrost key can never pose as a local account.

**A virtual key registered to an account** (pasted in the admin panel, or its
digest added to `api_keys` by hand) signs in as that account instead: the
session is revocable from `users.json` like any other, and lasts
`OCS_TOKEN_TTL_DAYS`. When `OCS_BIFROST_URL` is set, Bifrost must still report
the key active as well, so switching it off in Bifrost stops the next sign-in;
without it, the key is just an API key. A disabled account is refused whatever
Bifrost says.

Reusing a key from another service ties the two together: whoever obtains it
gets both. Only its unsalted SHA-256 is stored here, which is why pasted keys
need at least 20 characters — a real virtual key has 42.

There is no `users.json` entry to revoke, which is the trade-off: **disabling a
virtual key in Bifrost stops new sign-ins, not sessions already issued.** Those
live until `OCS_VK_TOKEN_TTL_DAYS` (7 by default), which is why they are short.
Unsetting `OCS_BIFROST_URL` invalidates all of them at once; rotating
`OCS_SESSION_SECRET` does too, along with everyone else's. The key itself keeps
being enforced by Bifrost for inference, so what lingers is read access to the
corporate configuration.

## The admin panel

Mounted only when `OCS_ADMIN_TOKEN` is set; otherwise `/admin` does not exist.
Treat the token like the `config/` directory it unlocks: it can change what runs
on every employee's machine (plugins, the installer).

- **One shared token**, compared in constant time and rate limited like the
  employee logins (`OCS_RATE_LIMIT_*`, bucket per client). Production refuses to
  start with a token shorter than 32 characters.
- **Browser sessions** are an HMAC-signed expiry in a cookie that is `HttpOnly`,
  `SameSite=Strict`, `Path=/admin`, and `Secure` whenever the base URL is https.
  The signing key is derived from `OCS_SESSION_SECRET` *and* the admin token, so
  rotating either ends every panel session. The cookie never contains the token.
- **CSRF**: requests riding on the cookie must also send `X-OCS-Admin: 1`.
  Another origin cannot add that header without a CORS preflight, and this
  server answers none.
- **The page** is static HTML with an external script and stylesheet under
  `default-src 'none'; script-src 'self'; style-src 'self'; connect-src 'self';
  frame-ancestors 'none'`, plus `X-Frame-Options: DENY`, `no-store` and
  `nosniff`. The script builds the DOM with `textContent` only — a test fails if
  `innerHTML` ever appears.
- **Secrets stay out of the browser**: password hashes and API key digests are
  never returned; a new API key is shown exactly once. Old versions of
  `users.json` in the history can be restored but not read. The history
  directory is `0700` and its files `0600`.
- **Session tokens of employees do not open the panel**, and the panel does not
  appear in `/openapi.json`.
- **Audit**: every change is logged as `admin <action> from <ip>`.

What the panel does not give you is per-person accountability: there is one
token. If several people administer the server, put `/admin` behind your SSO
proxy and keep the token as the second factor.

## The server is trusted by every client

An employee who logs in grants this server the ability to set their agents,
permissions, MCP servers, providers and plugin list. That is the point, and it is
also the blast radius. Specifically:

- **A `{file:…}` reference in the configuration is read from the employee's
  disk** by the harness. Combined with an `mcp` header or a provider `baseURL`,
  that is an exfiltration path. `configdoc.py` refuses to serve a document
  mentioning `~/.ssh`, `~/.aws`, `~/.gnupg` or `/etc/shadow`, but that is a
  tripwire against accidents, not a sandbox. Review changes to
  `config/opencode.jsonc` like you review code.
- **`plugins[]` entries execute in the harness process.** An npm spec served
  from here runs on every employee machine. Pin versions.
- **`bootstrap/install.sh` runs arbitrary shell** on first login. Same review
  bar as any deployment script.

Write access to `config/` is equivalent to code execution on every employee's
machine. Protect it accordingly: review, and no shared credentials to the host.

## Employees can opt out

Because the corporate document is the lowest-priority source, an employee can
override any scalar key and can drop the corporate plugin with
`"plugins": ["-<package>"]`. This is inherent to "never overwrite local
settings" — the two cannot both be true. If a setting must be mandatory, enforce
it outside OpenCode: MDM, a managed image, or CI checks.

## Hardening checklist

- [ ] `OCS_ENV=production`, `OCS_BASE_URL` on https, TLS terminated in front
- [ ] `OCS_SESSION_SECRET` from `python -m opencode_config_server.secret`, held
      in a secret store and not in the image
- [ ] `config/users.json` outside the image (`OCS_USERS_FILE`) or mounted
      read-only, `0600`
- [ ] `config/` mounted read-only — unless the admin panel is enabled, which
      needs it writable (`docker-compose.admin.yml`)
- [ ] `OCS_ADMIN_TOKEN` unset, or 32+ characters from
      `python -m opencode_config_server.secret --admin` and kept in a secret
      store; `/admin` reachable only from your network or behind SSO
- [ ] container as non-root, `cap_drop: ALL`, `read_only: true`
- [ ] access logs for `/skills/` redacted
- [ ] `OCS_TRUST_PROXY` true only behind a proxy that sets `X-Forwarded-For`
- [ ] rate limiting or lockout at the edge if you run more than one replica
- [ ] employees told to keep `~/.config/opencode-corp/credentials` at `0600`
      (the login script refuses to read it otherwise)

# Variables

How to put values that differ per employee — provider API keys above all — into
the corporate configuration without ever writing them in `opencode.jsonc`.

Verified against OpenCode v2.1.1: `packages/core/src/config.ts`
(`loadWellknownEntry`), `packages/core/src/config/variable.ts`,
`packages/cli/src/services/service-config.ts`.

## The four placeholders

| Write this | Filled in by | With |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `{server_url}` | this server, before sending | this server's public address (`OCS_BASE_URL`) |
| `{session_token}` | this server, as `{env:OPENCODE_CORP_SESSION}` | the employee's session token. Only useful to reach this server (the skills URL uses it) |
| `{env:NAME}` | this server if it defines `NAME`, otherwise OpenCode on the employee's machine | see [Where `{env:NAME}` comes from](#where-envname-comes-from) |
| `{file:~/path}` | OpenCode on the employee's machine | the contents of that file, trimmed. Use `~/` or absolute paths; a relative path resolves against nothing useful in a remote document. A missing file gives an empty string |

They work inside any string of the document: whole values or parts of them
(`"{env:BIFROST_URL}/v1"`). They are never resolved inside comments.

## Where `{env:NAME}` comes from

The rule everywhere: **the employee's own values win over the company's.**

```
{env:NAME}
   │
   ├─ 0. the employee defines NAME themselves        → left as is: theirs is used
   │     (reported by their last `opencode auth login`)
   ├─ 1. a value for this employee on the Variables page    ─┐ filled in by this
   ├─ 2. a value for everyone on the Variables page          ─┘ server, per request
   │
   │     (otherwise the placeholder travels as is)
   │
   ├─ 3. OPENCODE_CORP_SESSION only: the employee's session token
   ├─ 4. the environment of the OpenCode process on the machine
   └─ 5. empty string
```

Steps 0–2 happen here, every time an employee's OpenCode fetches the
configuration (at start-up and every 10 minutes). Steps 3–5 are OpenCode's own
rules for remote documents.

Step 0: at each login, the login command asks for the names of the variables
that apply to the employee (`GET /bootstrap/names`), checks which ones they
already define, and reports those names — never their values — back
(`POST /bootstrap/own-env`). "Already define" means present in the environment
OpenCode runs with (the same one step 4 reads), or in its service configuration,
with a value the login did not put there itself. A change on the machine counts
from the next login.

The file on disk keeps the placeholder; only the copy sent to that employee
carries the value.

## When the employee and the company define the same thing

| Same name or field in… | Wins | How |
| --- | --- | --- |
| the employee's local `opencode.json` and the corporate document | the employee | OpenCode ranks the corporate document below every local file (checked: a local `providers.<id>.settings.apiKey` replaces the corporate one) |
| the employee's environment and a variable on the Variables page | the employee | step 0 above |
| the employee's OpenCode service environment and a "machine" variable | the employee | the login never sets or unsets a variable it did not set itself |
| a "machine" variable the login set, later edited by the employee | the employee | from then on it is theirs: not overwritten, not unset |
| a skill in the employee's own skills folder and a corporate skill with the same name | the employee | the login reports the names it finds in `~/.config/opencode/skill(s)/`, and the server leaves those out of their catalogue (OpenCode would otherwise load the corporate one last and use it) |
| a skill folder inside one project (`.opencode/skills/`) and a corporate skill with the same name | **the company** | the login cannot see every project; give corporate skills names nobody else would use |
| `skills` and `instructions` lists | both | OpenCode adds every document's entries together; an employee can add their own, not remove the company's |

The panel shows, per user, which names they define themselves, and **Preview**
lists them for the chosen user.

## Defining values: the Variables page

Admin panel → **Variables**:

- **Everyone**: shared values, e.g. `BIFROST_URL`.
- **Per user**: pick an employee, add their own values, e.g. their
  `OPENAI_API_KEY`. A user's value replaces the shared one with the same name.
- **Secret**: once saved, the panel never shows the value again — only that it
  is set. To change it, type a new one; to keep it, leave the field empty.
- Names look like environment variables: letters, digits and `_`.
  `OPENCODE_CORP_SESSION` is reserved (the session token).

Changes reach employees on their next refresh, within 10 minutes, without
anyone signing in again. **Preview** on the Configuration page shows the
document exactly as a chosen employee receives it (secret values masked), plus
the names left for their machine to resolve.

Deleting a user deletes their variables. The file is `config/variables.json`;
see [Security](#security).

## Example: a personal OpenAI key per employee

Configuration (Advanced tab, or the file):

```jsonc
"providers": {
  "openai": {
    "settings": { "apiKey": "{env:OPENAI_API_KEY}" }
  }
}
```

Variables → Per user → `ana.ruiz` → `OPENAI_API_KEY` = her key, secret.

Ana receives her key; an employee without a value gets `{env:OPENAI_API_KEY}`
untouched and OpenCode falls back to `OPENAI_API_KEY` on their machine, if any.

## Example: Bifrost as the LLM gateway

Each employee calls Bifrost with their own virtual key, so Bifrost's budgets and
rate limits apply per person. Bifrost's OpenAI-compatible endpoint is
`<bifrost>/v1` and takes the virtual key as `Authorization: Bearer sk-bf-…`
(checked against a real Bifrost: `GET /v1/models` answers 200 with the key, 401
without).

```jsonc
"providers": {
  "bifrost": {
    "name": "Bifrost",
    "package": "@opencode/ai/providers/openai-compatible",
    "settings": {
      "baseURL": "{env:BIFROST_URL}/v1",
      "apiKey": "{env:BIFROST_API_KEY}"
    },
    "models": {
      "claude-sonnet": { "modelID": "anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5", "name": "Claude Sonnet (Bifrost)" },
      "gpt": { "modelID": "openai/gpt-5", "name": "GPT-5 (Bifrost)" }
    }
  }
},
"model": "bifrost/claude-sonnet"
```

- The key of `models` (`claude-sonnet`) is how OpenCode names the model
  (`bifrost/claude-sonnet`); `modelID` is what Bifrost receives. List what your
  Bifrost serves with `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $VK" <bifrost>/v1/models`.
- Variables → Everyone → `BIFROST_URL` = `https://bifrost.corp` (not secret).
- Variables → Per user → each employee → `BIFROST_API_KEY` = their virtual key
  (secret). Registering the same key under Users → API keys lets them sign in
  to this server with it too.

    "corp-docs": {
      "type": "remote",
      "url": "https://docs.corp/mcp",

## Values that must exist on the machine itself

`{env:…}` filled in here only reaches the configuration document. A plugin, a
local MCP server or a shell command that reads `process.env.NAME` needs the
variable in the environment of the OpenCode process itself. OpenCode's
background service keeps its own environment, which you can change by hand:

```bash
opencode service set env HINDSIGHT_API_KEY 'value'   # stored in ~/.config/opencode/service.json, 0600
opencode service get env                              # list them
opencode service unset env HINDSIGHT_API_KEY
```

Or tick **Also set it in the environment of OpenCode on the machine** on the
variable, and the login does it for each employee:

1. After signing in, the login command asks `GET /bootstrap/env` for that
   employee's machine variables (user values over shared ones, as above).
2. It works out, read-only, what to change: set the ones whose value differs,
   skip the ones the employee defines themselves, unset the ones it set before
   that the server no longer sends — only if they still hold the value it put
   there. Nothing to change means no restart.
3. If there is something to change it starts a detached job and returns.
   `opencode service set env` stops the service, and the login runs inside
   that service, so the job waits a few seconds for the login to finish.
4. The job runs `opencode service set env` / `unset env` and starts the service
   again if it was running.

What that means in practice:

- It is applied at **`opencode auth login`**, not every 10 minutes: re-run the
  login on a machine to pick up a change.
- Applying a change **restarts OpenCode** on that machine, interrupting sessions
  in progress there.
- **The employee's values are never touched**: one they set themselves is kept
  (and the login says so), and one the login set and they later changed becomes
  theirs.
- It needs the `opencode` binary of the running service (found from the process
  that runs the login, else `opencode` on `PATH`; set
  `OPENCODE_CORP_OPENCODE_BIN` to force one). `OPENCODE_CORP_SKIP_ENV=1` skips
  both this and step 0.
- `opencode auth login --standalone` uses a private server, not the service:
  the values land in the service's environment for its next start.
- Values pass as arguments to `opencode service set env`, so another account on
  the same machine could glimpse them in the process list for a moment.
- The login's bookkeeping lives in `~/.config/opencode-corp/env.managed`: the
  names it set, with a digest of each value, which is how it recognises its own.

The variable then also satisfies `{env:NAME}` in the configuration, at step 4 of
the order above — but there is no need to tick it for that.

On Windows the PowerShell login does the same, with a hidden PowerShell process
as the detached job. Windows PowerShell 5.1 mangles arguments that contain
double quotes when calling programs, so keep `"` out of machine values.

Mind paths that differ between platforms: the corporate document is the same
for every machine, and `HOME` is not set on Windows. Use a per-user variable
(`{env:PROJECTS_DIR}`) rather than `{env:HOME}/…`.

Do not call `opencode service set env` from `bootstrap/install.sh` (or
`install.ps1`): the
installer runs inside the login, inside that same service, so stopping it aborts
the login.

## Security

- Never write a key literally in the configuration: every employee who signs in
  can read the whole document. The panel warns about literal `apiKey`,
  `authToken`, `accessToken`, `bearerToken` and secret-looking header values.
- `config/variables.json` holds the values in clear, `0600`, like `users.json`
  holds password hashes: keep `config/` out of git (`.gitignore` already
  excludes both) and out of backups you would not trust with the keys.
- A value is sent only to the employee it belongs to (or to everyone, for shared
  ones), over TLS, with `Cache-Control: no-store`. OpenCode keeps the last
  configuration it received on that machine.
- Values cannot contain `{env:…}` or `{file:…}`: OpenCode substitutes again
  after this server, and a value must not be able to make machines read local
  files.
- Old versions of `variables.json` in the history can be restored, never
  displayed. The log records which variable changed, never its value.
- Sessions opened with an unregistered Bifrost key (`vk:<name>`) belong to no
  account, so they only get the values for everyone.
- What an employee defines themselves reaches this server as **names only**
  (`config/.state/employee-env.json`, 0600), never values.

## Where values end up on the employee's machine

| What | Where | When it changes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The session token | OpenCode's database, `~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db`, table `credential` (file 0600) | at each `opencode auth login` |
| The configuration with the values filled in | the same database, table `kv`, key `wellknown:config:<server>`; also in memory while OpenCode runs | at start-up and every 10 minutes; kept as is if the server is unreachable |
| Machine variables | `~/.config/opencode/service.json`, `env` (0600), in the service's environment once it restarts | at `opencode auth login`, only if they changed |

These are OpenCode's defaults on every platform, under the user's home;
`XDG_DATA_HOME` and `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` move them
(`packages/util/src/global-roots.ts`).

# Estándares de Codificación Corporativos

## Principios Generales

1. **Tipado Estricto**: Todo código nuevo debe usar tipado estático (TypeScript, Python con type hints, Go, Rust)
2. **Documentación**: Funciones públicas deben tener docstrings/comentarios JSDoc
3. **Testing**: Cobertura mínima 80% para código nuevo
4. **Linting**: Código debe pasar todos los linters configurados (ESLint, ruff, golangci-lint, clippy)

## Estilo de Código

### TypeScript/JavaScript
- Usar `const` por defecto, `let` solo cuando sea necesario
- Preferir `interface` sobre `type` para objetos
- Usar `unknown` en lugar de `any`
- Evitar `as any` y `@ts-ignore` - usar type guards
- Funciones flecha para callbacks, `function` para métodos de clase

### Python
- Usar `from __future__ import annotations`
- Type hints obligatorios en funciones públicas
- Usar `dataclasses` / `pydantic` para DTOs
- Evitar `Any` - usar `Protocol` o generics
- `ruff` como linter principal

### Go
- Seguir `gofumpt` para formato
- `golangci-lint` con configuración estricta
- Manejo de errores explícito - no `panic` en código de producción
- Usar `context.Context` en todas las operaciones I/O

### Rust
- `clippy` con `deny(warnings)`
- `rustfmt` estándar
- Preferir `Result<T, E>` sobre `Option<T>` para errores
- Usar `thiserror` para errores, `anyhow` solo en binarios

## Arquitectura

- **Separación de responsabilidades**: Capas claras (domain, application, infrastructure)
- **Inyección de dependencias**: Usar interfaces/ports, no implementaciones concretas
- **Inmutabilidad**: Preferir estructuras inmutables
- **Principio de responsabilidad única**: Un archivo = una responsabilidad

## Seguridad

- **Nunca** commitear secrets, API keys, tokens
- Usar variables de entorno para configuración sensible
- Validar y sanitizar toda entrada de usuario
- Usar prepared statements / ORM para queries SQL
- Implementar rate limiting en APIs públicas

## Git

- Commits atómicos y descriptivos (Conventional Commits)
- Branches: `feature/`, `fix/`, `chore/`, `docs/`, `refactor/`
- PRs requieren review y CI passing
- `main` protegido - solo merge via PR

# Flujo de Trabajo Git Corporativo

## Estructura de Branches

```
main                 # Protegida, solo merge via PR
  ├── develop        # Integración continua (opcional)
  ├── release/*      # Ramas de release (release/v1.2.0)
  ├── hotfix/*       # Fixes críticos en producción (hotfix/bug-description)
  ├── feature/*      # Nuevas funcionalidades (feature/JIRA-123-description)
  ├── fix/*          # Bug fixes (fix/JIRA-456-description)
  ├── chore/*        # Mantenimiento (chore/update-deps, chore/refactor-auth)
  └── docs/*         # Documentación (docs/api-update)
```

## Convención de Commits (Conventional Commits)

```
<type>[scope opcional]: <descripción corta>

[cuerpo opcional]

[footer opcional]
```

### Types
- `feat`: Nueva funcionalidad
- `fix`: Corrección de bug
- `docs`: Cambios en documentación
- `style`: Formato, punto y coma, etc (sin cambio de lógica)
- `refactor`: Refactorización sin cambio de funcionalidad
- `perf`: Mejora de rendimiento
- `test`: Añadir o corregir tests
- `chore`: Mantenimiento, build, deps, tooling
- `ci`: Cambios en CI/CD
- `security`: Cambios de seguridad

### Ejemplos
```
feat(auth): add OAuth2 PKCE support

fix(api): handle null response in user endpoint

chore(deps): update anthropic-sdk to v0.25.0

security(deps): patch CVE-2024-XXXX in lodash

refactor(core): extract validation logic to separate module
```

# Políticas de Seguridad Corporativas

## Gestión de Secrets

### Prohibido
- Hardcodear passwords, API keys, tokens en código
- Commitear archivos `.env`, `.env.local`, `secrets.yaml`
- Compartir credenciales por Slack, email, chat
- Usar secrets de producción en desarrollo

### Obligatorio
- Usar gestor de secrets corporativo (HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, 1Password CLI)
- Rotar credenciales cada 90 días máximo
- Revocar acceso inmediato al detectar compromiso
- Auditoría trimestral de accesos

## Dependencias

### Análisis de Vulnerabilidades
- Escaneo automático en CI/CD (OWASP Dependency Check, Snyk, Trivy)
- Bloquear merge si hay vulnerabilidades `CRITICAL` o `HIGH` sin mitigar
- Actualizar dependencias mensualmente (Dependabot/Renovate)
- Revisar licencias - solo licencias aprobadas (MIT, Apache-2.0, BSD-3)

### Supply Chain
- Verificar firmas de paquetes (npm provenance, sigstore)
- Usar lockfiles commitidos (`package-lock.json`, `go.sum`, `Cargo.lock`)
- Pinnear versiones en Dockerfiles (`FROM node:20.12.0@sha256:...`)
- Base images oficiales y actualizadas

## Red y Comunicaciones

### TLS/SSL
- TLS 1.3 obligatorio en producción
- Certificados válidos y renovados automáticamente (Let's Encrypt / cert-manager)
- HSTS activado en todos los endpoints HTTPS
- Certificate Transparency monitoring

### APIs
- Autenticación obligatoria (OAuth2/OIDC, mTLS, API Keys con rotación)
- Rate limiting por cliente/IP
- Validación estricta de entrada (schema validation)
- Logging de accesos anómalos (sin loggear datos sensibles)

## Datos

### Encriptación
- **En tránsito**: TLS 1.3 en todas las comunicaciones
- **En reposo**: AES-256 para bases de datos, discos, backups
- **En uso**: Confidential Computing donde aplique (AWS Nitro, Azure Confidential VMs)

### Clasificación
- **Pública**: Documentación, marketing
- **Interna**: Código, configs, logs anonimizados
- **Confidencial**: PII, credenciales, claves criptográficas
- **Restringida**: Secretos de producción, claves raíz

### Retención
- Logs de acceso: 1 año
- Logs de auditoría seguridad: 7 años
- Backups: 30 días (diarios), 1 año (mensuales)
- Datos de clientes: Según contrato/regulación (GDPR, CCPA)

## Acceso y Autenticación

### Principio de Mínimo Privilegio
- Acceso just-in-time (JIT) para producción
- Roles definidos por equipo/proyecto
- Revocación automática al cambio de rol/salida
- Revisiones de acceso trimestrales

### MFA
- Obligatorio para: VPN, consolas cloud, GitHub/GitLab, gestores de secrets
- Hardware keys (YubiKey) para admins de infraestructura

## Incidentes

### Respuesta
- Plan de respuesta a incidentes documentado y probado
- Runbooks para escenarios comunes
- Comunicación clara: stakeholders, clientes, reguladores
- Post-mortem blameless en < 48h para incidentes SEV-1/2

### Reporte
- Canal dedicado para reporte de vulnerabilidades (security@empresa.com)
- Bug bounty program para investigadores externos
- SLA de respuesta: 24h (ack), 72h (triage), 30d (fix crítico)

## Cumplimiento

- SOC 2 Type II anual
- ISO 27001 certificación
- GDPR/CCPA compliance para datos personales
- PCI DSS si procesa pagos
- Auditorías internas trimestrales
